newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Jospin takes France on cautious left turn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Jospin takes France on cautious left turn.

text.p: France's Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin began the hard task of reconciling his election promises with economic reality on Thursday, announcing a modest boost to the minimum wage and a gradual move to a 35-hour week.

In a keynote policy speech to parliament that won a standing ovation and delighted trade unions but dented share prices and bonds, Jospin declared: "The commitments made before the French people during the election campaign will be honoured."
But he made clear that change would take time because of what he called the "serious" state of public finances.
After a passionless debate, the National Assembly gave the government of Socialists, Communists and ecologist Greens a vote of confidence by 297 to 252 votes with two abstentions.

Jospin said a mini-budget and a promised national conference on wages, jobs and working hours would have to wait until September to give the government time to study an independent audit of public deficits due in mid-July.
The audit is expected to show how far France has strayed from reducing its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for the single European currency from 1999.
The prime minister said he was committed to launching the euro on time but, significantly, he made no mention of meeting the criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU).

He stressed that the euro must go hand in hand with economic solidarity, vowed to step up France's drive to shift the European Union's priorities from austerity to jobs and pledged to create the conditions for more vigorous growth at home.

"The feebleness of growth is a problem facing the whole of Europe. There must therefore be a common response. In this perspective, we reaffirm our determination to achieve economic and monetary union at the deadline provided for by the treaty.
"But you cannot share a currency without creating economic solidarity. The independence of a (European) central bank...does not mean a political vacuum," he said.

In a moment of irony, Gaullist opposition floor leader Philippe Seguin, who led the "no" campaign in France's 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty, warned Jospin against using the audit as an excuse to go back on European commitments.
Jospin's defeated Gaullist predecessor. Alain Juppe, did not speak in the debate but his aides issued a statement saying he had left public finances in an improving condition.

"Any increase in public spending and any interruption in the privatisation process can only make more hazardous respecting the commitments renewed in Amsterdam to enable France to qualify for European economic and monetary union," the statement said.

The Paris stock exchange index ended the day 0.44 percent down in nervous trading. Shares in companies involved in privatisations and restructurings fell, while retail shares rose against the trend on the boost to purchasing power.
Swept to power in an upset election win three weeks ago, Jospin vowed to give "absolute priority" to a campaign pledge to find 700,000 jobs for young people. He did not say how or when.

There were groans of disappointment from the Socialist, Communist and ecologist coalition benches when he announced that the minimum wage, now 6,406 francs a month, would be increased by four percent, far less than trade unions and the Communist party had demanded.
Stung by the reaction, Jospin said that given price rises of less than one percent, this was the biggest boost in purchasing power for the low-paid in 15 years.

Welfare benefits for the poorest citizens and pensions would be increased but family allowances would be means-tested and targeted at the lower-paid and middle-income earners. A one-off cash payment to low-income families with school age children in September would be quadrupled to 1,600 francs.

Jospin vowed to end his centre-right predecessors' policy of cutting jobs in the civil service and to stabilise the overall tax burden. "If growth allows it, my target is to reduce it in the longer term," he said.
Economist Philippe Brossard of ABN AMRO bank said the modest minimum wage rise "shows policy remains slow and cautious..it shows they want to achieve things over a five year period".
But he said it was not clear how Jospin would fund what he called the "long catalogue of expansion measures".

In the austere, schoolmasterly tone that is his hallmark, Jospin pledged to restore republican values, introduce morality lessons as well as civics in schools and revive the right of all people born on French soil to automatic citizenship.
"We must return to the republican spirit," he said. "Let's make a pact: a republican pact, a pact for development and for solidarity."

Pledging to change immigration and nationality laws enacted by the former centre-right government, he said: "Nothing is more alien to France than xenophobia and racism. France must define a firm, dignified immigration policy without renouncing its values or compromising its social balance."

Jospin promised to free the justice system from political meddling, leaving the appointment of investigating judges and prosecutors in the hands of an independent council and barring the Justice Ministry from intervening in individual cases.

He said the government did not favour the privatisation of telecommunications, electronics or aerospace companies, but left himself a loophole by accepting the need to adapt and form partnerships with other European companies.
